transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess what finally made me come in is that I can’t seem to stay seated when I’m supposed to. It sounds silly saying it out loud, but it’s become really noticeable. Like, during client interviews for work, I’ll get up to “just grab something” or check something or pace a little, even when I really should be sitting there listening. And I do tutoring sometimes, and even there I’ll find myself popping up out of the chair when the other person is talking.

It’s not just work, either. I’m in a book club, and everyone else can sit with their tea and talk through the discussion, and I’m the one standing up, moving around, adjusting things, going to look at the shelf—anything except just staying put. People have started commenting on it, not always unkindly, but enough that I’m aware of it now. I just feel like I can’t sit still and listen the way other adults seem to.
Do you feel restless when you're sitting and that's why you get up, or is it more that you just can't seem to stay seated?

It’s probably both, but the part that stands out is that I just don’t seem to stay seated when I’m expected to. I’ll tell myself, “Okay, just sit and listen,” and then before I really register it, I’m up—getting a file, checking something across the room, moving my chair, refilling water, whatever excuse my brain comes up with in the moment.

During client interviews it’s especially embarrassing because I know I’m supposed to look calm and attentive, and instead I’m sort of popping up and down like I can’t leave things alone. Same with tutoring—I should be sitting there while the other person works through something, but I keep finding reasons to stand up. And at book club, where there’s really no practical reason to be moving around, I’ll still end up wandering to the shelf or straightening things.

So, yes, there’s this uncomfortable “I need to move” feeling, but mostly what brings me in is that I keep leaving my seat when I’m supposed to stay put, and people are starting to notice that I can’t just sit and listen.
Do you feel anxious when you're sitting and trying to stay still?

I’m not sure I’d call it anxiety, exactly. I mean, I do get uncomfortable when I’m trying to sit still, but it doesn’t feel like worry in the usual sense, like I’m sitting there thinking something terrible is going to happen. It’s more… physical, maybe? Like this pressure to move, or this feeling that staying still takes way more effort than it should.

Sometimes I probably look tense, and I might feel a little self-conscious if I notice people noticing me, but the actual reason I get up doesn’t feel like fear. It’s not like I’m panicking in the chair. It’s more that sitting there quietly feels almost impossible after a bit, and then I’m up before I’ve really decided to be.
Do you find it hard to focus on what's being discussed when you're sitting still?

I’m not totally sure, honestly. I’ve been thinking about the getting-up part so much that I don’t know if I’ve paid enough attention to whether I’m also missing what people are saying.

I mean, sometimes if I’m forcing myself to stay still, I’m very aware of my body—like, “don’t move, don’t get up, just sit here”—and that can take up space in my head. But I don’t know that I can say clearly, yes, I can’t focus on the discussion. I’d have to think about it more. It’s more obvious to me that sitting still itself feels difficult, and then everything sort of revolves around that.
Do you find yourself easily distracted when you're trying to focus on something?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that, because I haven’t really tracked it in that way. I know that when I’m trying to focus on something, I can get kind of caught up in the effort of staying with it, if that makes sense, but I don’t know if I’d say I’m “easily distracted” in a clear, across-the-board way.

Like, I’d have to think about what counts as distracted. If you mean, do I notice every little sound or suddenly lose the thread constantly, I’m not sure. I can’t honestly say I’ve paid enough attention to that to give you a clean yes. What I notice more is the struggle around sitting still or staying settled, and then sometimes it’s hard to tell whether my mind wandered because I was distracted, or because I was so aware of trying to keep myself in one place.

So… I guess my answer is, maybe sometimes, but I don’t really know. It’s not the thing I’ve noticed most clearly.
Do you often act on impulse without thinking things through?

Yes… I think that’s probably fair to say. Not always in some dramatic way, but I do jump in before I’ve really thought through whether it’s my place.

At work, for example, if I hear the junior detectives talking through a lead, I’ll suddenly be in the conversation with questions or suggestions before anyone asked me. It can feel like I’m just trying to help, and in the moment the thought is right there, like, “Wait, did you check this?” or “No, ask it this way,” and I’m saying it before I’ve paused to see if they actually wanted input.

And it’s not just work. If I hear a neighbor talking in the hallway, I can kind of insert myself—ask a question, give advice, comment on something—and then a minute later I realize, oh, I just barged into someone else’s conversation. I don’t usually mean to be rude, but I can see how it comes across that way. It’s like the filter or the pause happens after I’ve already spoken, not before.
Have you noticed your impulsive behavior causing issues with your friends, family, or colleagues?

Yes. That’s actually the part that’s making me take it more seriously, because it’s not just, you know, “Oh, I talk too fast” or “I jump in sometimes.” It’s starting to cost me professionally.

In investigations, there have been times where I moved too quickly on what I thought was the important angle, and then later realized I’d missed a detail I should have caught. And that is… hard to admit, because my whole job depends on noticing details and listening carefully and not bulldozing past information just because I think I already see the shape of the thing.

Clients have gotten irritated with me too. Not always in a huge blowup way, but I can tell when I’ve interrupted too much or pushed them toward an answer before they were done explaining. Sometimes I’m trying to get to the relevant part, but from their side it probably feels like I’m rushing them or not really hearing them.

And with junior detectives, that’s been uncomfortable. I’ve noticed some of them are less willing to debrief with me now. They’ll keep it shorter, or they’ll talk to someone else first, because I think they feel steamrolled by me. Like if they bring me a lead, I’m already questioning it, redirecting it, telling them what to do, before they’ve even laid out what they found. I don’t mean it that way, but I can see why they’d pull back.

So yes, it’s causing issues. Mostly at work, but work is a big part of my life, and it’s starting to feel like my “just trying to help” instinct is damaging trust.
Do you have difficulty sustaining attention on tasks or activities?

I’m not sure I can give you a clean yes or no on that. I mean, I can sit with something for a while if I know exactly what I’m doing and why it matters, especially if there’s some urgency to it. But when you say “sustaining attention,” I’m not totally sure where the line is between normal fatigue or boredom and an actual problem.

With my work, tasks can be kind of uneven. Some parts pull you in because there’s a question to answer or a person to find or some inconsistency that keeps nagging at you. Other parts are just… sitting with records, reviewing notes, organizing information, going back over the same material again to make sure nothing was missed. And I know those parts can feel harder, but I don’t know if that means I have difficulty sustaining attention or if I just don’t like those parts as much.

I haven’t really tracked it closely enough to say, “Yes, this happens often.” I notice more when I’m restless or when I’m pushing to get to the next piece of things. Whether that’s attention exactly, I don’t know. I guess I’d say I’m aware that some tasks feel harder to stay with than others, but I’m not confident enough to call it a major attention problem.
Do you often find yourself fidgeting with your hands or feet when you're sitting still?

Yes, definitely. That’s one I notice a lot, especially when I’m forced to sit still at the computer for a long stretch.

If I’m combing through records or reading through pages of notes, my foot will be bouncing under the desk almost the whole time. Sometimes I don’t even realize I’m doing it until the chair is kind of shaking or I notice my leg is tired. Or I’ll be clicking a pen, tapping it, shifting in the chair, crossing and uncrossing my legs—just constantly adjusting myself.

And the frustrating part is it can actually interfere with what I’m doing. I’ll be reading something important, and because I’m moving around or fidgeting with something in my hands, I lose my place on the page or on the screen. Then I have to go back and find where I was, and that makes the whole task take longer. It’s not like I’m trying to be restless; it just seems to happen when I’m stuck sitting there.
Did you have trouble sitting still or acting on impulse when you were a child?

Yes. I mean, looking back, that was there pretty early. My grade-school report cards had that same kind of language over and over — “bright,” “capable,” “good ideas,” but also that I couldn’t stay in my seat, couldn’t wait my turn, was always up or blurting or moving before I was supposed to.

At the time I don’t think anyone framed it as anything serious. It was more like, “She’s energetic,” or “She needs to learn patience.” But my mother still jokes about it now. She says I treated every classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through, like I needed to get up and inspect everything instead of just sitting at my desk like the other kids.

And I do remember that feeling, vaguely — not in a dramatic way, but that sitting still when I wanted to move or speak felt almost unbearable sometimes. Like if I had a thought, waiting for the right moment felt impossible. So yes, that part didn’t just appear recently. It was definitely there when I was a kid.
Have you experienced these difficulties with sitting still and impulsivity consistently throughout your life, or have they varied in severity over time?

They’ve been there in some form for most of my life, but the severity definitely hasn’t been totally steady. Lately it’s been much more noticeable — I’d say for about the last eight months.

That lines up pretty closely with when I had to move out of my old apartment in Chicago. Since then, the sitting-still piece and the acting-before-I’ve-really-paused piece have felt harder to manage. It’s not that they appeared out of nowhere, because I can look back and see the same patterns earlier, but the volume got turned up after that move. Like I’m more aware of the restlessness now, and it feels more disruptive than it used to.
Do you think your difficulty staying seated and acting on impulse are more related to having too much energy or having trouble paying attention?

I think it feels more like having too much energy in my body, honestly. Not necessarily good energy, just… constant motion, like my motor doesn’t really shut off.

On days when I don’t have field work, you’d think I’d be able to relax or at least sit at home and be off duty for a while, but I’ll still go from unpacking boxes to reorganizing case files to suddenly deciding I need to run three errands. It’s almost like I’m chasing a lead even when there isn’t one. I’ll tell myself, “Okay, just sit down for a bit,” and then five minutes later I’m up doing something else because sitting there feels wrong somehow.

So yes, attention is probably part of it sometimes, but the staying-seated and impulse part feels more like this built-up drive to keep moving or act on whatever pops up next. I have a hard time just being still and off duty.
Do you think your main problem is that you can't focus or that you have too much energy and can't stay still?

It’s more the too-much-energy, can’t-stay-still side of it. I mean, I can have focus when there’s something to pursue, but the bigger problem is that I don’t seem to know how to just stop.

Even on days when I don’t have field work, when there’s no real reason to be “on,” I’ll still bounce from one thing to another — unpacking boxes, then reorganizing case files, then suddenly deciding I need to run errands. It feels like I’m chasing a lead even when there isn’t one. Like my body is still in work mode and I can’t quite switch it off.

So I wouldn’t say it’s mainly that I can’t focus. It’s more that sitting still feels almost unnatural, and being off duty is weirdly hard for me.
Do you think your main issue is more with not being able to pay attention or with being overly active and restless?

It’s definitely more the overly active and restless part. I can pay attention when there’s something concrete in front of me, especially if it feels urgent or interesting, but the thing that really wears me down is that I don’t seem to know how to be still.

Like, even on days when I don’t have field work — when technically I should be able to take the day slower — I’ll still keep moving from one thing to the next. I’ll start unpacking boxes, then suddenly I’m reorganizing case files, then I’m out the door running errands, and the whole time it feels like I’m chasing a lead even though there isn’t actually a lead to chase.

It’s like my body stays in work mode. I have a really hard time just being off duty. Sitting down and doing nothing feels almost uncomfortable, like I’m supposed to be getting up or handling something. So I’d say the main issue is the constant activity and restlessness, more than just not being able to pay attention.
Have your difficulties with sitting still and acting on impulse significantly interfered with your daily life or relationships?

Yes. I mean, I don’t like admitting that, because in my line of work you’re supposed to be sharp, measured, good at listening and putting pieces together. But it has started to cost me professionally.

There have been investigations where I’ve moved too fast — jumped in, acted on the next thing that occurred to me, pushed ahead before I’d really sat with all the details — and later I realized I missed something I should have caught. Not huge dramatic TV-type mistakes, but enough that it mattered. A detail in a statement, a timing issue, something in a file that I skimmed because I was already halfway out the door mentally and physically.

Clients notice too. I can get impatient in meetings, or I’ll interrupt because I think I know where they’re going, and sometimes they get irritated. I can tell when someone feels like I’m not giving them enough room, even if I’m trying to be helpful or efficient.

And with junior detectives, that’s been harder than I expected. Some of them don’t seem as willing to debrief with me now, because I think they feel steamrolled. I ask questions fast, I cut in, I’m already moving to the next angle before they’ve finished laying out what they saw. I don’t mean to shut them down, but I can see how it lands.

So yes, it’s not just annoying or embarrassing. It’s affecting the way I work with people and the quality of the work itself.
Have you experienced difficulties with sitting still and impulsivity consistently since you were a child?

Yes, it goes back pretty far. Grade school, definitely. My report cards were always some version of, “She’s bright, but she can’t stay in her seat,” or “has trouble waiting her turn.” I remember that phrase showing up so often it almost became part of my identity at school.

My mother still jokes about it, actually. She says I treated every classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through — like I was constantly up, looking around, needing to check something, ask something, move somewhere. At the time everyone acted like it was just me being energetic or impatient, but looking back, yes, the sitting still and waiting-my-turn part was there from when I was a kid.
Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder?

I’m not sure I have a clean answer to that. I mean, not in any formal, documented way that I can point to. I haven’t had someone sit me down and say, “This is officially what you have,” at least not that I remember.

I’ve had people suggest things over the years — teachers, family, even colleagues making comments — but that’s not the same as being evaluated or treated for it. And honestly, I think I brushed a lot of it off because I was functioning. I finished school, I built a career, I kept telling myself, “Well, if it were really a problem, I wouldn’t be able to do all this.”

So no, not formally treated, as far as I know. This is really the first time I’m trying to look at it directly instead of just working around it.
Do you think your difficulties are more with paying attention to details or with controlling your impulses and physical restlessness?

It’s more the impulse and restlessness side, I think. The attention-to-details part can get caught up in it, because if I’m already moving before I’ve really stayed with something, I can miss things. But what actually brings me in is that I keep getting up when I’m supposed to stay put.

It happens in client interviews, which is embarrassing because I’m supposed to be listening carefully and making them feel heard. I’ll stand up to grab something, pace a little, check a file, refill coffee I don’t even really need — and then I realize they’re watching me instead of talking. It’s like my body decides the meeting is too still before my brain has agreed.

And it’s not just work. I’ve done it in tutoring sessions too, and even at book club, which should be the most low-stakes sitting-and-listening situation imaginable. Someone will be making a point, and I’m up shifting chairs, going to the kitchen, looking at the shelf, anything. People have started noticing that I can’t just sit and listen, and that feels awful because I’m not trying to be rude. I just feel like I have to move.
Do you think your difficulties with impulsivity and restlessness are more pronounced in certain settings or situations?

Yes, definitely. It’s most obvious in situations where I’m supposed to remain seated and be quietly attentive for a stretch of time. Client interviews are probably the biggest one, because there’s this very clear expectation that I’m supposed to sit there, listen, take in what they’re saying, and not make myself the center of attention. And instead I’ll find myself standing up to get a file, or moving around the room, or checking something I don’t actually need to check right that second.

It also happens in tutoring sessions and even at book club, which feels almost ridiculous to say because those are not high-pressure in the same way. But if I’m expected to just sit and listen, that’s when it shows up. I start shifting, then I’m up out of the chair, going to the kitchen, looking at a shelf, rearranging where I’m sitting — and people notice. That’s what has been bothering me lately. It’s not just an internal feeling anymore; other people are starting to react to the fact that I can’t seem to stay put and just listen.
Do you often interrupt others or finish their sentences for them?

Yes. I do, and it’s one of those things I don’t always catch until a second too late.

It’s not always literally finishing someone’s sentence, though I probably do that sometimes. More often it’s that I hear part of a conversation and my brain just decides I should be in it. Like if the junior detectives are talking through a lead, I’ll jump in with questions or advice before anyone has asked me to. I’ll hear them say one detail and suddenly I’m standing there going, “Did you check this?” or “You should call so-and-so,” and only afterward do I realize they were still working it out themselves and I kind of barged in.

It happens outside work too. If a neighbor is talking in the hallway and I catch something that sounds like a problem I know how to solve, I’ll insert myself before I’ve really been invited. In the moment it feels helpful, like I’m contributing, but then afterward I’ll think, “Why did I do that? That wasn’t even my conversation.” It can feel embarrassing, because I don’t mean to be rude or take over, but I can see how it might come across that way.

doctor.question: Do you often find yourself fidgeting with your hands or feet when you're sitting still?

target_item.name: Fidgeting
target_item.manifestation: When I'm stuck at the computer combing through records, my foot is bouncing under the desk, I'm clicking a pen, or I'm shifting around so much that I lose my place in what I'm reading.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about fidgeting with hands or feet while sitting still.

patient.answer:
Yes, definitely. That’s one I notice a lot, especially when I’m forced to sit still at the computer for a long stretch.

If I’m combing through records or reading through pages of notes, my foot will be bouncing under the desk almost the whole time. Sometimes I don’t even realize I’m doing it until the chair is kind of shaking or I notice my leg is tired. Or I’ll be clicking a pen, tapping it, shifting in the chair, crossing and uncrossing my legs—just constantly adjusting myself.

And the frustrating part is it can actually interfere with what I’m doing. I’ll be reading something important, and because I’m moving around or fidgeting with something in my hands, I lose my place on the page or on the screen. Then I have to go back and find where I was, and that makes the whole task take longer. It’s not like I’m trying to be restless; it just seems to happen when I’m stuck sitting there.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms started in childhood
doctor.question: Did you have trouble sitting still or acting on impulse when you were a child?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: My grade-school report cards always said I was bright but couldn't stay in my seat or wait my turn, and my mother still jokes that I treated every classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether symptoms like trouble sitting still or impulsive behavior were present during childhood, which directly relates to onset before age 12.

patient.answer:
Yes. I mean, looking back, that was there pretty early. My grade-school report cards had that same kind of language over and over — “bright,” “capable,” “good ideas,” but also that I couldn’t stay in my seat, couldn’t wait my turn, was always up or blurting or moving before I was supposed to.

At the time I don’t think anyone framed it as anything serious. It was more like, “She’s energetic,” or “She needs to learn patience.” But my mother still jokes about it now. She says I treated every classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through, like I needed to get up and inspect everything instead of just sitting at my desk like the other kids.

And I do remember that feeling, vaguely — not in a dramatic way, but that sitting still when I wanted to move or speak felt almost unbearable sometimes. Like if I had a thought, waiting for the right moment felt impossible. So yes, that part didn’t just appear recently. It was definitely there when I was a kid.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms have been persistent across their lifetime
doctor.question: Have you experienced these difficulties with sitting still and impulsivity consistently throughout your life, or have they varied in severity over time?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been noticeably worse for about 8 months, since I had to move out of my old Chicago apartment.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the sitting-still and impulsivity difficulties have been consistent over life or have varied in severity over time, which is most directly about the duration/course of symptoms.

patient.answer:
They’ve been there in some form for most of my life, but the severity definitely hasn’t been totally steady. Lately it’s been much more noticeable — I’d say for about the last eight months.

That lines up pretty closely with when I had to move out of my old apartment in Chicago. Since then, the sitting-still piece and the acting-before-I’ve-really-paused piece have felt harder to manage. It’s not that they appeared out of nowhere, because I can look back and see the same patterns earlier, but the volume got turned up after that move. Like I’m more aware of the restlessness now, and it feels more disruptive than it used to.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are primarily related to attention deficit or hyperactivity
doctor.question: Do you think your difficulty staying seated and acting on impulse are more related to having too much energy or having trouble paying attention?

target_item.name: Constant_Activity
target_item.manifestation: On days when I don't have field work, I still move from unpacking boxes to reorganizing case files to running errands like I'm chasing a lead, and I have a hard time just being off duty.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the staying-seated and impulsive behavior feels more like excess energy/restless drive versus inattention, which most directly matches the constant 'on the go' symptom.

patient.answer:
I think it feels more like having too much energy in my body, honestly. Not necessarily good energy, just… constant motion, like my motor doesn’t really shut off.

On days when I don’t have field work, you’d think I’d be able to relax or at least sit at home and be off duty for a while, but I’ll still go from unpacking boxes to reorganizing case files to suddenly deciding I need to run three errands. It’s almost like I’m chasing a lead even when there isn’t one. I’ll tell myself, “Okay, just sit down for a bit,” and then five minutes later I’m up doing something else because sitting there feels wrong somehow.

So yes, attention is probably part of it sometimes, but the staying-seated and impulse part feels more like this built-up drive to keep moving or act on whatever pops up next. I have a hard time just being still and off duty.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are primarily driven by inattention or hyperactivity
doctor.question: Do you think your main problem is that you can't focus or that you have too much energy and can't stay still?

target_item.name: Constant_Activity
target_item.manifestation: On days when I don't have field work, I still move from unpacking boxes to reorganizing case files to running errands like I'm chasing a lead, and I have a hard time just being off duty.
target_item.reason: The question is directly asking whether the problem is mainly excess energy and inability to stay still, which matches being constantly active or driven by a motor.

patient.answer:
It’s more the too-much-energy, can’t-stay-still side of it. I mean, I can have focus when there’s something to pursue, but the bigger problem is that I don’t seem to know how to just stop.

Even on days when I don’t have field work, when there’s no real reason to be “on,” I’ll still bounce from one thing to another — unpacking boxes, then reorganizing case files, then suddenly deciding I need to run errands. It feels like I’m chasing a lead even when there isn’t one. Like my body is still in work mode and I can’t quite switch it off.

So I wouldn’t say it’s mainly that I can’t focus. It’s more that sitting still feels almost unnatural, and being off duty is weirdly hard for me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are primarily related to attention deficit or hyperactivity
doctor.question: Do you think your main issue is more with not being able to pay attention or with being overly active and restless?

target_item.name: Constant_Activity
target_item.manifestation: On days when I don't have field work, I still move from unpacking boxes to reorganizing case files to running errands like I'm chasing a lead, and I have a hard time just being off duty.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the main issue is inattentiveness versus being overly active and restless; this most directly matches constant activity/being driven by a motor.

patient.answer:
It’s definitely more the overly active and restless part. I can pay attention when there’s something concrete in front of me, especially if it feels urgent or interesting, but the thing that really wears me down is that I don’t seem to know how to be still.

Like, even on days when I don’t have field work — when technically I should be able to take the day slower — I’ll still keep moving from one thing to the next. I’ll start unpacking boxes, then suddenly I’m reorganizing case files, then I’m out the door running errands, and the whole time it feels like I’m chasing a lead even though there isn’t actually a lead to chase.

It’s like my body stays in work mode. I have a really hard time just being off duty. Sitting down and doing nothing feels almost uncomfortable, like I’m supposed to be getting up or handling something. So I’d say the main issue is the constant activity and restlessness, more than just not being able to pay attention.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms have caused significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning
doctor.question: Have your difficulties with sitting still and acting on impulse significantly interfered with your daily life or relationships?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It's starting to cost me professionally—I've missed details in investigations, irritated clients, and made junior detectives less willing to debrief with me because they feel steamrolled.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the sitting still and impulsivity difficulties have significantly interfered with daily life or relationships, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes. I mean, I don’t like admitting that, because in my line of work you’re supposed to be sharp, measured, good at listening and putting pieces together. But it has started to cost me professionally.

There have been investigations where I’ve moved too fast — jumped in, acted on the next thing that occurred to me, pushed ahead before I’d really sat with all the details — and later I realized I missed something I should have caught. Not huge dramatic TV-type mistakes, but enough that it mattered. A detail in a statement, a timing issue, something in a file that I skimmed because I was already halfway out the door mentally and physically.

Clients notice too. I can get impatient in meetings, or I’ll interrupt because I think I know where they’re going, and sometimes they get irritated. I can tell when someone feels like I’m not giving them enough room, even if I’m trying to be helpful or efficient.

And with junior detectives, that’s been harder than I expected. Some of them don’t seem as willing to debrief with me now, because I think they feel steamrolled. I ask questions fast, I cut in, I’m already moving to the next angle before they’ve finished laying out what they saw. I don’t mean to shut them down, but I can see how it lands.

So yes, it’s not just annoying or embarrassing. It’s affecting the way I work with people and the quality of the work itself.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms have been persistent since childhood
doctor.question: Have you experienced difficulties with sitting still and impulsivity consistently since you were a child?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: My grade-school report cards always said I was bright but couldn't stay in my seat or wait my turn, and my mother still jokes that I treated every classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the sitting-still and impulsivity difficulties have been present since childhood, which directly corresponds to onset prior to age 12.

patient.answer:
Yes, it goes back pretty far. Grade school, definitely. My report cards were always some version of, “She’s bright, but she can’t stay in her seat,” or “has trouble waiting her turn.” I remember that phrase showing up so often it almost became part of my identity at school.

My mother still jokes about it, actually. She says I treated every classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through — like I was constantly up, looking around, needing to check something, ask something, move somewhere. At the time everyone acted like it was just me being energetic or impatient, but looking back, yes, the sitting still and waiting-my-turn part was there from when I was a kid.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a specific attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder subtype
doctor.question: Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about prior diagnosis or treatment history for ADHD, but the provided symptom profile does not include any item covering past diagnosis or treatment.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I have a clean answer to that. I mean, not in any formal, documented way that I can point to. I haven’t had someone sit me down and say, “This is officially what you have,” at least not that I remember.

I’ve had people suggest things over the years — teachers, family, even colleagues making comments — but that’s not the same as being evaluated or treated for it. And honestly, I think I brushed a lot of it off because I was functioning. I finished school, I built a career, I kept telling myself, “Well, if it were really a problem, I wouldn’t be able to do all this.”

So no, not formally treated, as far as I know. This is really the first time I’m trying to look at it directly instead of just working around it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are primarily inattentive, hyperactive-impulsive, or a combination of both
doctor.question: Do you think your difficulties are more with paying attention to details or with controlling your impulses and physical restlessness?

target_item.name: Leaving_Seat
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that I keep getting up when I'm supposed to stay put—during client interviews, tutoring sessions, even book club—and people are starting to notice that I can't just sit and listen.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the main problem is hyperactive/impulsive restlessness rather than inattention, and this item best matches the patient’s difficulty staying seated when expected.

patient.answer:
It’s more the impulse and restlessness side, I think. The attention-to-details part can get caught up in it, because if I’m already moving before I’ve really stayed with something, I can miss things. But what actually brings me in is that I keep getting up when I’m supposed to stay put.

It happens in client interviews, which is embarrassing because I’m supposed to be listening carefully and making them feel heard. I’ll stand up to grab something, pace a little, check a file, refill coffee I don’t even really need — and then I realize they’re watching me instead of talking. It’s like my body decides the meeting is too still before my brain has agreed.

And it’s not just work. I’ve done it in tutoring sessions too, and even at book club, which should be the most low-stakes sitting-and-listening situation imaginable. Someone will be making a point, and I’m up shifting chairs, going to the kitchen, looking at the shelf, anything. People have started noticing that I can’t just sit and listen, and that feels awful because I’m not trying to be rude. I just feel like I have to move.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a specific ADHD subtype
doctor.question: Do you think your difficulties with impulsivity and restlessness are more pronounced in certain settings or situations?

target_item.name: Leaving_Seat
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that I keep getting up when I'm supposed to stay put—during client interviews, tutoring sessions, even book club—and people are starting to notice that I can't just sit and listen.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the restlessness and impulsivity are worse in particular settings or situations; the profile most directly tied to settings is leaving the seat during client interviews, tutoring sessions, and book club when staying seated is expected.

patient.answer:
Yes, definitely. It’s most obvious in situations where I’m supposed to remain seated and be quietly attentive for a stretch of time. Client interviews are probably the biggest one, because there’s this very clear expectation that I’m supposed to sit there, listen, take in what they’re saying, and not make myself the center of attention. And instead I’ll find myself standing up to get a file, or moving around the room, or checking something I don’t actually need to check right that second.

It also happens in tutoring sessions and even at book club, which feels almost ridiculous to say because those are not high-pressure in the same way. But if I’m expected to just sit and listen, that’s when it shows up. I start shifting, then I’m up out of the chair, going to the kitchen, looking at a shelf, rearranging where I’m sitting — and people notice. That’s what has been bothering me lately. It’s not just an internal feeling anymore; other people are starting to react to the fact that I can’t seem to stay put and just listen.

doctor.intent: Determine if symptoms meet criteria for ADHD, specifically assessing intent and impulsivity to differentiate between F90.0, F90.8, and F90.9
doctor.question: Do you often interrupt others or finish their sentences for them?

target_item.name: Interrupting_Intruding
target_item.manifestation: If I hear junior detectives discussing a lead or a neighbor talking in the hallway, I jump in with questions or advice before I've been asked, and afterward I realize I barged into someone else's conversation.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about interrupting others or finishing their sentences, which directly matches interrupting or intruding on others.

patient.answer:
Yes. I do, and it’s one of those things I don’t always catch until a second too late.

It’s not always literally finishing someone’s sentence, though I probably do that sometimes. More often it’s that I hear part of a conversation and my brain just decides I should be in it. Like if the junior detectives are talking through a lead, I’ll jump in with questions or advice before anyone has asked me to. I’ll hear them say one detail and suddenly I’m standing there going, “Did you check this?” or “You should call so-and-so,” and only afterward do I realize they were still working it out themselves and I kind of barged in.

It happens outside work too. If a neighbor is talking in the hallway and I catch something that sounds like a problem I know how to solve, I’ll insert myself before I’ve really been invited. In the moment it feels helpful, like I’m contributing, but then afterward I’ll think, “Why did I do that? That wasn’t even my conversation.” It can feel embarrassing, because I don’t mean to be rude or take over, but I can see how it might come across that way.
